sectionTitle: Common atmospheric pollutants and their sources

specStatements.text: The combustion of fuels is a major source of atmospheric pollutants.
Most fuels, including coal, contain carbon and/or hydrogen and may also contain some sulfur.

The gases released into the atmosphere when a fuel is burned may include carbon dioxide, water vapour, carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen. Solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons may also be released that form particulates in the atmosphere.
describe how carbon monoxide, soot (carbon particles), sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen are produced by burning fuels
predict the products of combustion of a fuel given appropriate information about the composition of the fuel and the conditions in which it is used.
Carbon monoxide is a toxic gas. It is colourless and odourless and so is not easily detected.
Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause respiratory problems in humans and cause acid rain.
Particulates cause global dimming and health problems for humans.

concepts.definition: The burning of a fuel in oxygen, which releases energy. The combustion of fuels is a major source of atmospheric pollutants.
A substance released into the atmosphere that harms human health or the environment. Burning fuels is a major source of these substances.
Most fuels, including coal, contain carbon and/or hydrogen. Some fuels also contain a small amount of sulfur.
Sulfur is present as an impurity in some fuels, such as coal. It is not a part of every fuel, so not every fuel produces sulfur dioxide when it burns.
Burning in a plentiful supply of oxygen. Carbon in the fuel is oxidised to carbon dioxide and hydrogen in the fuel is oxidised to water vapour.

Burning when the supply of oxygen is too small for the fuel to burn completely. As well as carbon dioxide and water vapour, carbon monoxide, solid carbon particles (soot) and unburned hydrocarbons may be released.
Carbon monoxide, CO, is produced when a fuel containing carbon burns in a supply of oxygen that is too small for complete combustion, so the carbon is only partly oxidised.
Soot is solid particles of carbon released when a fuel burns in too little oxygen and some of the carbon in the fuel is not oxidised at all.
Sulfur present as an impurity in the fuel is oxidised when the fuel burns: S + O2 → SO2. Fuels with no sulfur in them do not produce sulfur dioxide.

concepts.term: How oxides of nitrogen are produced
concepts.definition: At the high temperatures reached inside an engine, nitrogen and oxygen from the air react together to form oxides of nitrogen. The nitrogen comes from the air, not from the fuel.
Solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons released when a fuel is burned form particulates in the atmosphere.
Fuel molecules that leave the engine or burner without reacting. Together with solid particles they form particulates in the atmosphere.

Work from two pieces of information: which elements the fuel contains, and how much oxygen is available. Carbon gives carbon dioxide, and also carbon monoxide and carbon particles if oxygen is limited; hydrogen gives water vapour; sulfur gives sulfur dioxide; a high temperature in air gives oxides of nitrogen.
Carbon monoxide is a toxic gas. It is colourless and odourless and so is not easily detected.
Rain made acidic by sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen released into the atmosphere when fuels are burned.
Breathing problems caused in humans by sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen in the air.
A reduction in the amount of sunlight reaching the Earth's surface, caused by particulates in the atmosphere.
As well as causing global dimming, particulates in the air cause health problems for humans.

misconceptions.question: Where does the nitrogen in oxides of nitrogen from a car engine come from?
misconceptions.correct: From nitrogen in the air, which reacts with oxygen at the high temperature inside the engine.
misconceptions.misconception: The fuel must contain nitrogen, because you cannot get nitrogen out of a reaction unless it was in the fuel to start with.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that the carbon in carbon dioxide and the sulfur in sulfur dioxide both come from the fuel, and generalise the pattern to every pollutant.
misconceptions.correction: Air is about four-fifths nitrogen, and the engine draws air in as well as fuel. At the high temperature inside the engine that nitrogen reacts with oxygen. Oxides of nitrogen are the one pollutant here that does not come from the fuel.

misconceptions.question: Does every fuel produce sulfur dioxide when it burns?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only fuels that contain sulfur produce sulfur dioxide.
misconceptions.misconception: All fuels contain sulfur, so burning any fuel gives off sulfur dioxide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sulfur dioxide appears in every list of combustion pollutants, so students read the list as things that always come out rather than things that may come out.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says most fuels contain carbon and/or hydrogen and may also contain some sulfur. Sulfur is an impurity in some fuels, such as coal. If a question tells you the fuel is sulfur-free, no sulfur dioxide can form.

misconceptions.question: What causes incomplete combustion?
misconceptions.correct: A supply of oxygen that is too small for the fuel to burn completely.
misconceptions.misconception: Incomplete combustion happens because the fuel is dirty or impure, so it cannot burn properly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word incomplete is read as a fault in the fuel, and soot looks like dirt, which reinforces the idea.
misconceptions.correction: Incomplete combustion is about the conditions, not the purity of the fuel. A perfectly pure hydrocarbon burns incompletely if there is not enough oxygen, producing carbon monoxide and carbon particles.

misconceptions.question: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous in a home with a faulty boiler?
misconceptions.correct: It is toxic, and because it is colourless and odourless it is not easily detected.
misconceptions.misconception: You would smell carbon monoxide, or see the fumes, before it could do you any harm.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate dangerous gases with a smell or a visible haze, because that is true of many gases they meet in a laboratory, such as chlorine and bromine.
misconceptions.correction: Carbon monoxide has no colour and no smell. That is exactly why it is so hazardous: there is no warning that it is present.

misconceptions.question: Which gas released by burning fuels causes acid rain?
misconceptions.correct: Sulfur dioxide, together with oxides of nitrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon dioxide causes acid rain, because carbon dioxide is the main pollutant from burning fuels.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbon dioxide is the pollutant students hear about most, and they carry it across from the previous topic on the greenhouse effect into every question about environmental damage.
misconceptions.correction: In this specification acid rain is caused by sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen. Carbon dioxide is dealt with separately, as a greenhouse gas.

misconceptions.question: Which problem do particulates cause?
misconceptions.correct: Global dimming, and health problems for humans.
misconceptions.misconception: Particulates make the Earth warmer, because everything that comes out of a chimney adds to global warming.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every pollution effect gets collapsed into one heading, global warming, so the specific effect named for particulates is lost.
misconceptions.correction: Particulates cause global dimming, which means less sunlight reaches the Earth's surface. They also cause health problems for humans.

misconceptions.question: Is water vapour released when a fuel burns?
misconceptions.correct: Yes, whenever the fuel contains hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: Burning gives off carbon dioxide; water vapour is not really a product because water puts fires out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Water is thought of as the opposite of burning, so students resist listing it as something combustion makes.
misconceptions.correction: Hydrogen in the fuel is oxidised to water, which leaves as water vapour because the gases are hot. The specification lists water vapour among the gases released when a fuel is burned.

misconceptions.question: Is carbon monoxide always produced when a fuel containing carbon burns?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is produced when the supply of oxygen is too small for complete combustion.
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon always turns into carbon monoxide first and then into carbon dioxide, so carbon monoxide comes out every time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture combustion as a sequence of steps rather than as one reaction whose products depend on how much oxygen is available.
misconceptions.correction: In a plentiful supply of oxygen the carbon is fully oxidised and carbon dioxide is the carbon-containing product. Carbon monoxide is a sign that the oxygen supply was limited.

misconceptions.question: What is soot?
misconceptions.correct: Solid particles of carbon released when a fuel burns in too little oxygen.
misconceptions.misconception: Soot and carbon monoxide are the same thing, because both are the carbon that did not burn properly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are products of incomplete combustion and both are described using the word carbon, so the two are stored as one idea.
misconceptions.correction: Carbon monoxide is a gas, made of carbon and oxygen. Soot is solid carbon particles, with no oxygen in it, and it contributes to particulates in the atmosphere rather than acting as a toxic gas.

misconceptions.question: Do carbon monoxide and particulates cause acid rain?
misconceptions.correct: No. Acid rain is caused by sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything that comes out of an exhaust pipe or a chimney can cause acid rain, so carbon monoxide and particulates cause it too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Pollutants are learned as a single list rather than as separate substances with separate effects, so one effect is attached to all of them.
misconceptions.correction: Each pollutant has its own named effect. Carbon monoxide is toxic; particulates cause global dimming and health problems; only sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen are named as causes of acid rain.

misconceptions.question: What does global dimming mean?
misconceptions.correct: Less sunlight reaches the Earth's surface because of particulates in the atmosphere.
misconceptions.misconception: Global dimming means the Sun itself is giving out less light than it used to.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word global attaches to the Sun rather than to the atmosphere, and dimming sounds like a change in the source of the light.
misconceptions.correction: The Sun is unchanged. Particulates in the atmosphere are what reduce the sunlight reaching the surface, which is why global dimming is worst where fuels are burned heavily.

misconceptions.question: What products form when coke, which is almost pure carbon, burns?
misconceptions.correct: Carbon dioxide, and carbon monoxide and carbon particles if the oxygen supply is limited.
misconceptions.misconception: Burning any fuel gives carbon dioxide and water vapour, so coke gives water vapour too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The complete combustion of hydrocarbons is practised so often that the pair carbon dioxide and water becomes an automatic answer for every fuel.
misconceptions.correction: Water can only form if the fuel contains hydrogen. Coke is almost pure carbon, so no water vapour is produced. Always check which elements the fuel contains before listing the products.

misconceptions.question: How can unburned hydrocarbons contribute to particulates?
misconceptions.correct: They are released along with solid particles and form particulates in the atmosphere.
misconceptions.misconception: Unburned hydrocarbons are fuel vapour, so they are gases and cannot be part of particulates.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Particulate is taken to mean solid only, so anything that leaves the engine as a vapour is ruled out.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons may be released and that these form particulates in the atmosphere. Both are named as sources of particulates.

misconceptions.question: Does sulfur dioxide only form during incomplete combustion?
misconceptions.correct: No. Sulfur in the fuel is oxidised to sulfur dioxide however much oxygen is available.
misconceptions.misconception: Sulfur dioxide is a pollutant, and pollutants come from incomplete combustion, so plenty of air stops sulfur dioxide forming.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Incomplete combustion is taught as the cause of the pollutants carbon monoxide and soot, and the rule is then over-extended to every pollutant.
misconceptions.correction: More oxygen cannot help here, because sulfur dioxide is already the oxidised product. The only way to avoid it is to remove the sulfur from the fuel or the sulfur dioxide from the waste gases.

mcqs.stem: Air above a busy city contains carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and particulates. What do these three pollutants have in common?

options.text: They are all released by the combustion of fuels
options.rationale: The specification names the combustion of fuels as a major source of atmospheric pollutants, and all three are produced when fuels burn.

options.text: They are all gases formed by incomplete combustion
options.rationale: A student who treats particulates as a gas like carbon monoxide, and who thinks every pollutant is a product of incomplete combustion, sees this as the common feature.

options.text: They are all produced from sulfur impurities in fuels
options.rationale: Chosen by students who believe sulfur is present in all fuels and is behind all pollution from burning.

options.text: They are all formed from nitrogen and oxygen in air
options.rationale: Picked by students who have learned that air supplies the nitrogen for oxides of nitrogen and extend that origin to every pollutant.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes the composition of most fuels?

options.text: They contain carbon and/or hydrogen and always contain sulfur
options.rationale: Selected by students who read sulfur dioxide in the list of combustion products as proof that every fuel contains sulfur.

options.text: They contain carbon and/or hydrogen and may contain sulfur
options.rationale: This is what the specification states: most fuels, including coal, contain carbon and/or hydrogen and may also contain some sulfur.

options.text: They contain carbon and nitrogen and may also contain sulfur
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume the nitrogen in oxides of nitrogen must have come from inside the fuel.

options.text: They contain sulfur and oxygen and may also contain hydrogen
options.rationale: A student who remembers that fuels react with oxygen may wrongly place oxygen in the fuel itself rather than in the air.

mcqs.stem: A hydrocarbon fuel that contains no sulfur is burned in a plentiful supply of air. Which substances are released?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide only
options.rationale: Chosen by students who do not accept water vapour as a combustion product and who expect carbon monoxide alongside carbon dioxide.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, water vapour, sulfur dioxide
options.rationale: Picked by students who list sulfur dioxide automatically, ignoring the statement that this fuel contains no sulfur.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water vapour only
options.rationale: With plenty of oxygen the carbon is fully oxidised to carbon dioxide and the hydrogen to water vapour; there is no sulfur, so no sulfur dioxide.

options.text: Carbon monoxide and water vapour only
options.rationale: Selected by students who believe carbon monoxide is the normal carbon product of burning whatever the oxygen supply.

mcqs.stem: Carbon monoxide is found in the exhaust gases of a petrol engine. Why is it produced?

options.text: The fuel contains impurities that cannot be burned fully in air
options.rationale: Chosen by students who blame the fuel rather than the conditions for incomplete combustion.

options.text: The carbon in the fuel reacts with nitrogen from the hot air
options.rationale: Picked by students who know nitrogen reacts at high temperature and attach it to the wrong product.

options.text: Carbon always forms carbon monoxide before carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Selected by students who picture combustion as a fixed sequence of steps instead of one reaction that depends on oxygen supply.

options.text: The oxygen supply is too small for the fuel to burn completely
options.rationale: Carbon monoxide is a product of incomplete combustion, which happens when there is not enough oxygen to oxidise all the carbon to carbon dioxide.

mcqs.stem: Oxides of nitrogen are formed inside a car engine. Where does the nitrogen come from, and why does it react?

options.text: From the air, because the high temperature makes it react with oxygen
options.rationale: At the high temperatures reached inside the engine, nitrogen and oxygen from the air react together to form oxides of nitrogen.

options.text: From nitrogen compounds in the fuel, which are oxidised as it burns
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume every element in a pollutant must have been present in the fuel.

options.text: From the fuel, because incomplete combustion releases it from the fuel
options.rationale: Picked by students who treat incomplete combustion as the explanation for every exhaust pollutant.

options.text: From the air, because nitrogen dissolves in the water vapour formed
options.rationale: A plausible-sounding route for students who know the nitrogen comes from air but reach for dissolving rather than a reaction at high temperature.

mcqs.stem: A power station burns coal that contains a small amount of sulfur. How is sulfur dioxide produced?

options.text: The coal burns incompletely, so sulfur dioxide escapes from the coal
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume every pollutant is a consequence of incomplete combustion, and that the gas was already inside the coal.

options.text: The sulfur in the coal is oxidised to sulfur dioxide as the coal burns
options.rationale: Sulfur present as an impurity in the fuel reacts with oxygen when the fuel burns: S + O2 → SO2.

options.text: Sulfur in the air is oxidised at the high temperature of the furnace
options.rationale: Picked by students who transfer the air origin of oxides of nitrogen to sulfur dioxide as well.

options.text: Carbon dioxide from the burning coal reacts with sulfur in the air
options.rationale: Selected by students who invent a secondary reaction rather than accepting that the sulfur simply burns.

mcqs.stem: Black soot is deposited around the burner of a poorly adjusted gas heater. What is soot, and how has it formed?

options.text: A colourless gas, formed by burning in too little oxygen
options.rationale: Chosen by students who have merged soot with carbon monoxide into one product of incomplete combustion.

options.text: Solid carbon particles, formed when carbon reacts with nitrogen
options.rationale: Picked by students who reach for the nitrogen in the air whenever they must explain an extra product.

options.text: Solid carbon particles, formed by burning in too little oxygen
options.rationale: When the oxygen supply is limited, some carbon in the fuel is not oxidised at all and is released as solid carbon particles.

options.text: Solid sulfur particles, formed from the sulfur impurity in the fuel
options.rationale: Selected by students who assume sulfur is present in every fuel and is responsible for the visible dirt.

mcqs.stem: A fuel oil contains carbon, hydrogen and a small amount of sulfur. It is burned in a plentiful supply of air. Which products are formed?

options.text: Carbon monoxide, water vapour and sulfur dioxide
options.rationale: Chosen by students who give carbon monoxide as the carbon product even when told the air supply is plentiful.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, water vapour and carbon particles
options.rationale: Picked by students who expect soot from any dirty fuel and who forget that the sulfur must go somewhere.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, water vapour and oxides of sulfur
options.rationale: A vague answer from students who copy the phrase oxides of nitrogen and apply its form to sulfur instead of naming sulfur dioxide.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, water vapour and sulfur dioxide
options.rationale: With plenty of air, carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide, hydrogen to water vapour and the sulfur impurity to sulfur dioxide.

mcqs.stem: Coke is a fuel that is almost pure carbon. A sample is burned in a limited supply of air. Which products would you expect?

options.text: Carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and carbon particles
options.rationale: With carbon as the only element present and a limited air supply, the carbon is oxidised to a mixture of carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide, and some is released unburned as particles.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and water vapour
options.rationale: Chosen by students who add water vapour out of habit, without checking that the fuel contains no hydrogen.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide and carbon particles
options.rationale: Picked by students who assume any solid fuel like coke must give off sulfur dioxide.

options.text: Carbon monoxide and carbon particles only
options.rationale: Selected by students who take limited supply of air to mean that no carbon dioxide at all can form.

mcqs.stem: An engine burns sulfur-free petrol in a plentiful supply of air. Which pollutant is still likely to be released, and where does it come from?

options.text: Sulfur dioxide, from the sulfur present in the petrol
options.rationale: Chosen by students who list sulfur dioxide reflexively and ignore the word sulfur-free in the stem.

options.text: Oxides of nitrogen, from the air drawn into the engine
options.rationale: Neither removing sulfur nor supplying plenty of air prevents nitrogen and oxygen in the air reacting at the high temperature inside the engine.

options.text: Carbon monoxide, from the carbon in the petrol
options.rationale: Picked by students who believe carbon monoxide is produced whenever a carbon fuel burns, whatever the oxygen supply.

options.text: Soot particles, from petrol that leaves unburned
options.rationale: Selected by students who expect soot from any engine rather than only when the oxygen supply is limited.

mcqs.stem: Homes with gas boilers are advised to fit a carbon monoxide alarm. Why can people not rely on their own senses instead?

options.text: It has a faint smell that most people do not recognise
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume any toxic gas gives some warning through its smell.

options.text: It is a solid particulate, so it settles out of the air
options.rationale: Picked by students who have confused carbon monoxide with soot and treat it as a solid.

options.text: It has no colour and no smell, so it is not easily detected
options.rationale: The specification states that carbon monoxide is colourless and odourless and so is not easily detected, which is why it is so hazardous.

options.text: It is only harmful to people who already have asthma
options.rationale: Selected by students who transfer the respiratory effects of sulfur dioxide onto carbon monoxide.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of pollutants released by burning fuels causes acid rain?

options.text: Carbon monoxide and oxides of nitrogen
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat carbon monoxide as an all-purpose harmful exhaust gas responsible for acid rain.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide
options.rationale: Picked by students who carry carbon dioxide across from the greenhouse effect into every environmental problem.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and particulates
options.rationale: Selected by students who attach every named effect to the pollutants they hear about most often.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
options.rationale: These are the two pollutants the specification names as causes of acid rain.

mcqs.stem: Air beside a busy road contains sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen. What harm do these gases do to people who breathe them in?

options.text: They cause respiratory problems in humans
options.rationale: The specification states that sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause respiratory problems in humans as well as acid rain.

options.text: They are harmless unless dissolved in rain
options.rationale: Chosen by students who remember only the acid rain effect and assume the gases are safe to breathe.

options.text: They are toxic but cannot be detected at all
options.rationale: Picked by students who transfer the colourless and odourless description of carbon monoxide onto these gases.

options.text: They cause global dimming above large cities
options.rationale: Selected by students who attach global dimming to gases rather than to particulates.

mcqs.stem: Which two effects does the specification link to particulates in the atmosphere?

options.text: Acid rain and health problems for humans
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think anything released from a chimney contributes to acid rain.

options.text: Global dimming and health problems for humans
options.rationale: These are exactly the two effects the specification gives for particulates.

options.text: Global warming and health problems for humans
options.rationale: Picked by students who collapse every atmospheric effect into global warming.

options.text: Global dimming and acid rain in nearby areas
options.rationale: Selected by students who know the dimming effect but add acid rain because the pollution is local and visible.

options.text: The Sun gives out less light than before
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read dimming as a change in the Sun rather than in the atmosphere.

options.text: The average temperature of the Earth rises
options.rationale: Picked by students who assume any global effect of pollution must mean warming.

options.text: Less sunlight reaches the Earth's surface
options.rationale: Global dimming is the reduction in sunlight reaching the surface, and the specification attributes it to particulates.

options.text: Rainwater slowly becomes more acidic
options.rationale: Selected by students who cannot separate the named effects and pick the environmental problem they know best.

mcqs.stem: A diesel engine releases solid carbon particles and unburned hydrocarbons. What do these form in the atmosphere, and what do they cause?

options.text: Acid rain, which damages trees and lakes
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assign acid rain to every pollutant leaving an exhaust pipe.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, which causes global warming
options.rationale: Picked by students who assume all carbon released ends up as carbon dioxide and warms the planet.

options.text: A toxic gas that is not easily detected
options.rationale: Selected by students who treat unburned hydrocarbon vapour as a gas that cannot form particulates, so choose a gas-based effect.

options.text: Particulates, which cause global dimming
options.rationale: The specification states that solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons form particulates, and that particulates cause global dimming and health problems.
